terms.def: The free-energy cost of a substituent sitting axial rather than equatorial on cyclohexane, in kcal/mol. A tert-butyl group's A-value (about 5) is large enough to lock the ring with it equatorial.

A carbon bonded to two OR groups, made from an aldehyde or ketone and two alcohols (or a diol) with acid, removing water. Acetals survive base and nucleophiles and are hydrolyzed by aqueous acid, so they protect carbonyls.
Alkylate the enolate of ethyl acetoacetate, then hydrolyze and decarboxylate: the result is a methyl ketone, CH₃COCH₂R.
The conjugate base of a terminal alkyne, R–C≡C⁻, made with NaNH₂. It is a strong nucleophile that forms C–C bonds by SN2 with methyl and primary halides.
Superimposable on its mirror image. Any molecule with a plane of symmetry (or a center of symmetry) is achiral.
Two acyl groups joined through one oxygen, R–CO–O–CO–R. It is the second most reactive carboxylic acid derivative, after acid chlorides.
R–CO–Cl, the most reactive carboxylic acid derivative, made from a carboxylic acid with SOCl₂. It reacts with water, alcohols and amines to give acids, esters and amides.
Ka, the equilibrium constant for an acid giving its proton to water, HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻. A larger Ka means a stronger acid.

A substituent that donates electron density to a benzene ring, making it react faster than benzene in EAS, such as –OH, –NH₂, –OR or alkyl. A deactivating group withdraws density and slows the reaction.
ΔG‡, the free-energy gap between the reactants and the transition state of a step. A higher barrier means a slower step.
The group R–C(=O)–, a carbonyl attached to one carbon group, as found in every carboxylic acid derivative.
The cation R–C≡O⁺, an acyl group stabilized by the oxygen's lone pair. It is the electrophile in Friedel–Crafts acylation and does not rearrange.

The two ways to add across a conjugated system. In 1,2-addition the pieces bond to adjacent atoms; in 1,4-addition they bond to the two ends (C1 and C4) and the remaining double bond moves to the middle.
A polymer made by joining monomers, usually alkenes, without losing any atoms, such as polyethylene or polystyrene.
A reaction in which two pieces add across a π bond, turning it into two new σ bonds, such as HBr adding to an alkene.
The single product formed when two species combine without losing any atoms, especially a Lewis base bonding to a Lewis acid through the base's lone pair.
A compound with an –OH group bonded to an sp³ carbon, R–OH.
A compound whose carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen, R–CHO.
An aldol reaction followed by loss of water, usually on heating, to give an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound.
An enolate (or enol) adds to the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde or ketone, giving a β-hydroxy carbonyl compound.
A monosaccharide whose open-chain form is an aldehyde, such as glucose. A ketose has a ketone instead, such as fructose.
A hydrocarbon with only single bonds; an open-chain alkane has the formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
A hydrocarbon containing a carbon–carbon double bond, C=C.
The conjugate base of an alcohol, RO⁻, such as methoxide or ethoxide. Alkoxides are strong bases and good nucleophiles.
A substituent made by removing one hydrogen from an alkane, named with the ending -yl: methyl, ethyl, propyl. It is often written R.
A compound with a halogen bonded to an sp³ carbon, written R–X. The C–X carbon is δ+ and X can leave, so alkyl halides are the classic substrates for substitution and elimination.
A hydrocarbon containing a carbon–carbon triple bond, C≡C.
A compound with two C=C bonds sharing one carbon, C=C=C. The two π bonds are perpendicular, so an allene with two different groups on each end is chiral without a stereocenter.

Describes the position next to a C=C: an allylic carbon is bonded to an alkene carbon and is sp³ in the neutral molecule. A cation, radical or anion there is stabilized by resonance: carrying the charge or the unpaired electron makes that carbon sp², so its p orbital overlaps with the π bond.

The carbon next to a functional group. In carbonyl chemistry it is the carbon bonded to the C=O carbon; in eliminations it is the carbon carrying the leaving group. The beta (β) carbon is the next one out.
In mass spectrometry, breaking the bond next to a carbonyl carbon (or next to the carbon bearing O or N), which gives a stabilized cation such as an acylium ion.
A hydrogen on the α carbon of a carbonyl compound. It is unusually acidic (pKa about 20 for a ketone) because its removal gives a resonance-stabilized enolate.
A compound with an amino group and a carboxylic acid on the same (α) carbon, H₂N–CHR–COOH. The 20 common amino acids differ in their side chain R; all but glycine are chiral.
An elimination in which both leaving groups come off the same carbon, as when Cl₃C⁻ loses Cl⁻ to give dichlorocarbene. An E2 is a β-elimination: the two groups leave from neighboring carbons.
Replacing an α hydrogen of a carbonyl compound with a halogen. With acid it goes through the enol and stops after one; with base it goes through the enolate and continues until every α H is replaced.
A carbonyl compound with a C=C between its α and β carbons, conjugated with the C=O, such as an enone. It is electrophilic at both the carbonyl carbon and the β carbon.
A nucleophile that can react at two different atoms, such as an enolate, which can bond through carbon or oxygen.
A carboxylic acid derivative with a nitrogen bonded to the carbonyl carbon, R–CO–NR′₂. (The same word is also used for the anion R₂N⁻, as in sodium amide.)
A derivative of ammonia in which one, two or three hydrogens are replaced by carbon groups: RNH₂, R₂NH or R₃N. The nitrogen lone pair makes amines bases and nucleophiles.
Having both a polar, water-loving part and a nonpolar, water-avoiding part, like soaps and phospholipids.
Able to act as either an acid or a base. Water is amphoteric: it gives H⁺ to bases and accepts H⁺ from acids.
The extra energy when bond angles are forced away from their ideal values, such as the 60° C–C–C angles in cyclopropane instead of 109.5°.
Aminobenzene, C₆H₅NH₂. It is a much weaker base than an alkylamine because its nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the ring.
An atom or molecule with a negative charge: it has more electrons than protons.
The carbon that was the carbonyl carbon in a sugar's open-chain form (C1 of an aldose). In the ring it is the hemiacetal or acetal carbon, and it is a new stereocenter.
Cyclic sugar diastereomers that differ only at the anomeric carbon. In a D-sugar's Haworth projection, the α anomer has the anomeric OH down (trans to CH₂OH) and the β anomer has it up.
An addition in which the two new groups bond to opposite faces of the π bond, as in Br₂ addition. In syn addition they bond to the same face.
The staggered conformation in which the two largest groups are 180° apart. For butane it is the most stable conformation.
Addition in which the non-hydrogen group ends up on the less substituted carbon, as in hydroboration–oxidation or HBr with peroxides.

Two bonds on neighboring atoms that lie in one plane and point in opposite directions (dihedral angle 180°). E2 needs the β-H and the leaving group arranged this way; on a cyclohexane both must be axial.
Describes a ring that is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated but has 4n π electrons. It is less stable than a comparable open chain, so such molecules avoid being planar if they can.
A molecular orbital with a node between the two nuclei, higher in energy than the orbitals that formed it. Electrons that enter it weaken the bond; it is written σ* or π*.
The resonance-stabilized carbocation formed when an electrophile adds to an aromatic ring; one ring carbon is sp³ and carries both the H and the E.
A checklist for comparing acids by the stability of their conjugate bases, applied in order: Atom (which atom holds the charge), Resonance, Induction, Orbital (hybridization of the lone pair).
Describes a ring that is cyclic, planar and fully conjugated with 4n + 2 π electrons (2, 6, 10...). Such rings are unusually stable, like benzene.
The number of protons in an atom's nucleus. It identifies the element: every carbon atom has atomic number 6.
Stereoisomers that can be separated because rotation around a single bond is blocked, as in some biaryls with bulky ortho groups.
Electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s, then 2s, then 2p, then 3s, and so on.
A bond on a chair cyclohexane that points straight up or down, parallel to the ring's axis. Axial directions alternate up and down around the ring.
A diazonium ion, a weak electrophile, attacks a strongly activated ring such as a phenol or aniline, joining the two rings through –N=N–. The products are often brightly colored azo dyes.
Approach of a nucleophile to a carbon from the side directly opposite the leaving group, 180° away, into the large lobe of the C–LG σ* orbital. It is required in SN2.

A peroxyacid turns a ketone into an ester (a cyclic ketone into a lactone) by inserting an oxygen between the carbonyl carbon and the group with the higher migratory aptitude. The migrating group keeps its configuration.
Hydrogen bonding between bases on two antiparallel strands: A pairs with T (U in RNA) through two hydrogen bonds, and G pairs with C through three.
The tallest peak in a mass spectrum, set to 100% intensity. It belongs to the most abundant ion, which is not necessarily the molecular ion.
A = εcl: absorbance equals the molar absorptivity times concentration times path length, so absorbance is proportional to concentration.
The shape of an atom with two bonds and two lone pairs, such as the oxygen in water, with a bond angle near 104.5°.
C₆H₆, a flat six-membered ring of sp² carbons with six π electrons spread evenly around it; the parent aromatic compound.
The substituent C₆H₅CH₂–, a phenyl ring attached through a CH₂.
Describes the carbon directly attached to a benzene ring. Benzylic cations, radicals and anions are stabilized by resonance with the ring, so benzylic positions react readily.

A very reactive intermediate: a benzene ring with an extra, strained π bond, made by eliminating HX from an aryl halide with a very strong base such as NaNH₂. A nucleophile can add at either end, so two products may form.
A hydrogen on a carbon next to the carbon that holds the leaving group (the β carbon). It is the hydrogen removed in an elimination.
A compound with two C=O groups on either side of one carbon (a 1,3-dicarbonyl), such as a β-keto ester or a malonic ester. The H's on that middle carbon are unusually acidic (pKa about 9 to 13).

Reduction of an aromatic ring with Na or Li in liquid ammonia and an alcohol, giving a non-conjugated cyclohexa-1,4-diene. An electron-donating group ends up on a remaining C=C; an electron-withdrawing group on an sp³ carbon.
A removable group, often SO₃H, put on a ring position temporarily so that a reaction is forced to happen elsewhere.
A higher-energy cyclohexane shape with eclipsed bonds and two flagpole hydrogens that clash across the ring. Twisting it slightly gives the somewhat lower-energy twist-boat.
The tert-butoxycarbonyl group, a carbamate that protects an amine. It is removed with acid, such as trifluoroacetic acid.
The dipole of a single polar bond, drawn in chemistry as an arrow pointing toward the δ− atom with a cross at the δ+ end.
The energy needed to break a particular bond homolytically, giving two radicals. A larger value means a stronger bond.
A bridgehead carbon of a small bicyclic ring cannot be part of a double bond, because the p orbitals could not line up without severe strain.
A three-membered ring cation in which a bromine bridges two carbons, formed when Br₂ adds to an alkene. Attack from the back side opens it, so the two bromines end up anti.
A proton (H⁺) donor.
A proton acceptor. It needs a lone pair, or occasionally a π bond, to bond to the incoming H⁺.
The angle, about 107° to the C=O bond, at which a nucleophile approaches a carbonyl carbon, aiming into the π* orbital.
NMR of the carbon-13 nuclei in a compound. With proton decoupling each unique carbon gives one line, spread over about 0 to 220 ppm; carbonyl carbons appear furthest downfield.

The rules for ranking groups at a stereocenter or double bond: the atom of higher atomic number wins; ties are broken at the first point of difference moving outward; a double bond counts its atoms twice.
A group R–O–CO–NR′₂, half ester and half amide. Boc and Cbz are carbamates that protect amines; polyurethanes are linked by carbamates.
A carbon with three bonds, one lone pair and a −1 formal charge. Carbanions are very strong bases and nucleophiles.

A neutral carbon with two bonds and two nonbonding electrons, six valence electrons in all, such as :CH₂ or :CCl₂. In a singlet carbene the pair shares one orbital and the p orbital is empty, so it adds to a C=C in one syn step; a triplet carbene has two unpaired electrons and adds stepwise, not stereospecifically.
A reagent that transfers a carbene unit without ever releasing a free carbene, such as ICH₂ZnI in the Simmons–Smith reaction.
The carbon that bears the OH group in an alcohol.
The tetrahedral intermediate, with an OH and an amine nitrogen on the same carbon, formed when an amine adds to a carbonyl. It loses water to give an imine or enamine.

A carbon with three bonds, no lone pair, six valence electrons and a +1 charge. It is trigonal planar with an empty p orbital; stability runs 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl, and resonance (allylic, benzylic) stabilizes it further.
A polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone, or a compound that hydrolyzes to them: sugars, starch and cellulose.
A carbon double-bonded to an oxygen, C=O. The oxygen pulls electron density away, leaving the carbonyl carbon δ+ and electrophilic.
The gem-diol R₂C(OH)₂ formed when water adds to a C=O. The equilibrium lies on the hydrate side only for very electrophilic carbonyls such as formaldehyde.
RCOO⁻, the conjugate base of a carboxylic acid. Its negative charge is shared equally by the two oxygens through resonance.
A compound with the carboxyl group, –COOH: a C=O and an OH on the same carbon. Typical pKa values are 4 to 5.
A compound R–CO–Y that can be turned into another by swapping Y in nucleophilic acyl substitution: acid chlorides, anhydrides, esters and amides. Nitriles share their oxidation level.
A substance that speeds a reaction by opening a lower-energy path and is regenerated at the end. It does not change the position of the equilibrium.
Addition of H₂ across a C=C or C≡C on a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Pt or Ni. Both hydrogens add to the same face (syn addition).
An atom or molecule with a positive charge: it has fewer electrons than protons.
The benzyloxycarbonyl group, a carbamate that protects an amine and is removed by hydrogenolysis (H₂, Pd/C).

A growing radical takes an H atom from another molecule, which ends its chain and starts a new one. When it takes an H from its own backbone (backbiting), growth carries on from there and leaves a branch.
Polymerization in which monomers add one at a time to a reactive chain end (a radical, cation or anion), so long chains appear early while most monomer is unreacted.
The most stable shape of cyclohexane, in which every C–C–C angle is close to 109.5° and every bond is staggered, so the ring has essentially no strain.
The position of an NMR signal, δ, in ppm from the TMS reference at 0. Nuclei near electronegative atoms or in aromatic rings are deshielded and appear at higher δ (downfield).
Describes nuclei that are interchanged by symmetry or by fast rotation, so they have identical surroundings and give one NMR signal.
A reagent's preference for reacting with one functional group over another in the same molecule, such as NaBH₄ reducing a ketone but leaving an ester alone.
Not superimposable on its mirror image, like a left hand. A chiral molecule and its mirror image are enantiomers.
The part of a molecule that absorbs UV or visible light, usually a conjugated π system.
Descriptors for two groups on a ring or a double bond: cis means on the same side, trans on opposite sides.
An ester enolate attacks a second ester by nucleophilic acyl substitution, giving a β-keto ester. A full equivalent of base is needed, because deprotonating the product drives the reaction.

The [3,3] sigmatropic rearrangement of an allyl vinyl ether on heating, which gives a carbonyl compound with a C=C between the third and fourth carbons from the C=O. The new C=O makes it effectively irreversible. Not the same reaction as the Claisen condensation.
Conversion of a C=O into CH₂ with zinc amalgam, Zn(Hg), in hot concentrated HCl. It suits molecules that tolerate strong acid.
Describes a step in which bonds break and form at the same time, through a single transition state with no intermediate.
A polymer formed by reactions that release a small molecule, such as water, an alcohol or HCl, each time a link forms; polyesters and polyamides are examples.
A written formula that lists each carbon with the hydrogens attached to it, in order, such as CH₃CH₂OH, with parentheses for branches.
The fixed spatial arrangement of groups at a stereocenter or double bond. Unlike a conformation, it can change only by breaking and remaking bonds.
One of the shapes a molecule can take by rotating around single bonds, without breaking any bond. Conformations interconvert rapidly, so they are not separate compounds.
Comparing the energies of a molecule's conformations, usually by adding up its strain interactions, to decide which conformation it mostly occupies.
The species a base becomes when it gains a proton. NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of NH₃.
An acid and the base it becomes on losing H⁺, which differ by exactly one proton, such as H₂O and OH⁻.
Addition of a nucleophile to the β carbon of an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl (1,4-addition). The enolate formed is then protonated at the α carbon. Soft nucleophiles prefer it.
The species an acid becomes when it loses a proton. The more stable the conjugate base, the stronger the acid.
Overlap of p orbitals on three or more adjacent atoms, as in alternating single and double bonds, which lets electrons spread over the whole system and lowers its energy.
Both ends of a π system turning the same way, both clockwise or both counterclockwise, as an electrocyclic ring forms or opens. Thermal reactions of 4n π electrons go this way.
Compounds with the same molecular formula but atoms joined in a different order, such as butane and 2-methylpropane.
A synthesis that builds large pieces separately and joins them late, which gives a higher overall yield than adding pieces one at a time in a long line.
Heating an amine oxide causes a syn elimination through a five-membered cyclic transition state, giving an alkene and a hydroxylamine.
The [3,3] sigmatropic rearrangement of a hexa-1,5-diene on heating, through a chair-shaped six-atom transition state. It is reversible and favors the more substituted diene.
A polymer made from two or more different monomers; the units can be arranged at random, alternating, or in blocks.
The electrons in an atom's inner, filled shells. They are held tightly and take no part in bonding.
J, the spacing in Hz between the peaks of a split NMR signal. Two hydrogens that split each other share the same J; for alkene H's, trans J is larger than cis.
A bond in which two atoms share a pair of electrons. Each line in a Lewis or skeletal structure is one shared pair.

A palladium-catalyzed reaction that joins an organic halide or triflate to an organometallic partner through a cycle of oxidative addition, transmetalation and reductive elimination (the Heck reaction instead uses alkene insertion and β-hydride elimination).
A covalent bond (or bridge) connecting two polymer chains. A few cross-links make a rubber elastic; many make a rigid network.
An aldol between two different carbonyl compounds. It gives one main product only when one partner cannot form an enolate (such as benzaldehyde) or one enolate is made first with LDA.
A large cyclic polyether whose oxygens wrap around a metal cation, as 18-crown-6 does K⁺. Holding the cation frees its anion to react, even in nonpolar solvents.
The fraction of a polymer whose chains are packed in ordered regions. More crystalline polymers are stiffer, stronger and more opaque; amorphous regions are disordered.
An acyl azide, heated, loses N₂ and rearranges to an isocyanate, which water turns into a primary amine with one fewer carbon.
An arrow that shows one electron pair moving: its tail starts on a lone pair or a bond, and its head points to the atom or bond position where the pair ends up.
A compound with an OH and a CN on the same carbon, made by adding HCN (with a little cyanide as catalyst) to an aldehyde or ketone. It adds one carbon to the chain.
A reaction in which two π systems join to form a ring, making two new σ bonds. The Diels–Alder reaction is a [4+2] cycloaddition.
A saturated hydrocarbon ring, named by putting cyclo- in front of the alkane with the same number of carbons, as in cyclohexane.
Turning a C=C into a cyclopropane ring by adding one carbon across it, from a carbene or a carbenoid. Both new bonds form in one step on one face, so the alkene's cis or trans geometry is kept.

Labels for sugars and amino acids read from a Fischer projection with the most oxidized carbon at the top. For a sugar, look at the OH on the stereocenter furthest from the carbonyl; for an amino acid, look at the NH₂ on the α carbon. Pointing right is D; pointing left is L.
A covalent bond in which both electrons came from the same atom, as when a Lewis base donates its lone pair to a Lewis acid. Once formed it is an ordinary covalent bond.
Dicyclohexylcarbodiimide, a coupling reagent that activates a carboxylic acid (as an O-acylisourea) so an amine can attack it and form an amide.
Loss of CO₂. β-Keto acids and malonic acids lose CO₂ easily on heating through a six-membered cyclic transition state that gives an enol.
Orbitals with the same energy, such as the three 2p orbitals of an atom.
The number of repeat units in a polymer chain, n. Molar mass ≈ n × the mass of the repeat unit.
The number of rings plus π bonds in a molecule, worked out from its formula as (2C + 2 + N − H − X) ÷ 2. Each one costs two hydrogens compared with a saturated open chain.
Loss of a water molecule. Acid-catalyzed dehydration turns an alcohol into an alkene, by E1 for secondary and tertiary alcohols.
Elimination of HX, usually by E2 with a strong base. Two successive dehydrohalogenations of a dihalide with NaNH₂ make an alkyne.
The spreading of electrons, and any charge they carry, over several atoms through overlapping p orbitals. Delocalization lowers energy, which is why resonance stabilizes.
Loss of a protein's folded 3D shape, by heat, pH change or solvents, without breaking its peptide bonds.
Breaking a polymer back into its monomers or small pieces, for example by hydrolysis or methanolysis of a polyester; the basis of chemical recycling.
A ¹³C NMR experiment that sorts carbons by how many hydrogens they carry. In DEPT-135, CH and CH₃ point up, CH₂ points down and carbons with no H vanish; DEPT-90 shows only CH.
A hypervalent iodine reagent (DMP) that oxidizes primary alcohols to aldehydes and secondary alcohols to ketones under mild, neutral conditions.
Stereoisomers that are not mirror images, such as cis and trans alkenes or compounds that differ at some but not all stereocenters. They have different physical properties.
Describes two groups for which replacing each in turn gives a pair of diastereomers. They are chemically different and can give separate NMR signals.

terms.def: Steric strain between an axial substituent and the two axial hydrogens (or groups) on the same face, two carbons away on either side.
Ar–N₂⁺ X⁻, made from a primary aromatic amine with NaNO₂ and HCl at 0 °C. N₂ is a superb leaving group, so the ring position can be turned into many other groups.
Diisobutylaluminum hydride, a bulky hydride reagent that reduces an ester or a nitrile only as far as the aldehyde when used cold (−78 °C), with one equivalent.

The carbene :CCl₂, made in the flask from chloroform and a strong base such as KOC(CH₃)₃ by an α-elimination. It adds to an alkene to give a 1,1-dichlorocyclopropane. :CBr₂ from CHBr₃ is made the same way.
An intramolecular Claisen condensation of a diester, giving a five- or six-membered cyclic β-keto ester.

A concerted [4+2] cycloaddition between a conjugated diene in its s-cis conformation and a dienophile, forming a cyclohexene with two new σ bonds in one step. It is stereospecific and usually favors the endo product.
A compound with two C=C bonds. They are conjugated when separated by one single bond, isolated when separated by at least one sp³ carbon, and cumulated when they share a carbon (an allene).
The alkene or alkyne partner in a Diels–Alder reaction. Electron-withdrawing groups on it, such as C=O or CN, make it react faster.
The angle between a bond on the front carbon and a bond on the back carbon, as seen in a Newman projection.

A measure of charge separation: the size of the separated charge times the distance between the charges, in debyes (D). A molecule's net dipole is the vector sum of its bond dipoles, so symmetric molecules such as CO₂ can have none.
Attractions between the permanent dipoles of polar molecules, the δ+ end of one lining up with the δ− end of another.
The way a substituent already on a benzene ring controls both how fast the ring reacts in EAS and which position (ortho, meta or para) the next group goes to.
An imaginary bond-breaking step in retrosynthesis that corresponds to a real forward reaction.
The two ends of a π system turning opposite ways, one clockwise and one counterclockwise, as an electrocyclic ring forms or opens. Thermal reactions of 4n + 2 π electrons go this way.
Reduction by sodium or lithium in liquid ammonia, which adds electrons one at a time. It turns an internal alkyne into the trans (E) alkene.
An S–S bond formed by oxidizing two cysteine thiols. It links parts of a protein chain, or separate chains, together.
Two shared electron pairs between two atoms: one σ bond and one π bond. Both atoms are usually sp² and the bond cannot rotate.
Labels for a double bond: rank the two groups on each carbon by CIP priority. If the higher-priority groups are on the same side it is Z, on opposite sides E. E is not always trans.
Unimolecular elimination: the leaving group departs to form a carbocation, then a weak base removes a β-hydrogen. It is not stereospecific, can rearrange, and usually gives the Zaitsev product.

Elimination through the conjugate base: an acidic hydrogen (often α to a C=O) is removed first to give a carbanion or enolate, which then expels a leaving group from the next carbon, such as OH⁻ in an aldol condensation.
Bimolecular elimination: in one concerted step a base removes a β-hydrogen while the leaving group departs, forming a C=C. The H and leaving group must be anti-periplanar; rate = k[base][substrate].
A conformation in which the bonds on the front carbon line up with those on the back (dihedral angle 0°). It is an energy maximum because of torsional strain.
A peptide-sequencing method that removes and identifies the N-terminal residue one at a time, as a phenylthiohydantoin, using phenyl isothiocyanate.
A polymer that stretches and springs back, typically amorphous, lightly cross-linked and used above its glass transition temperature.
A pericyclic reaction in which the two ends of a conjugated π system join with a new σ bond to make a ring, or the reverse ring opening. Hexa-1,3,5-triene closing to cyclohexa-1,3-diene is one.
A list of the orbitals an atom's electrons occupy, with the number in each, such as 1s² 2s² 2p² for carbon.
Anything that occupies a direction around an atom: a lone pair, an unpaired electron or a bond to another atom. A double or triple bond counts as one group.
An atom's pull on the electrons in a bond it shares. It increases up a group and to the right across a period; fluorine is the most electronegative element, and carbon and hydrogen are close.
An electron-poor species that accepts a pair of electrons from a nucleophile to form a new bond: a δ+ carbon, a carbocation, H⁺ or a Lewis acid.
A reaction in which an electrophile replaces an H on an aromatic ring: the ring's π electrons attack E⁺ to give an arenium ion (the slow step), then loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity.
Separating charged molecules by their movement in an electric field: cations travel toward the cathode, anions toward the anode, and a molecule at its pI does not move.
A reaction that removes atoms or groups from adjacent carbons and forms a π bond between them, such as loss of HBr to make an alkene.
A compound with an amine nitrogen on a C=C (ene + amine), made from an aldehyde or ketone and a secondary amine. Like an enolate, it is nucleophilic at the α carbon.
The percentage of the major enantiomer minus the percentage of the minor one. It equals optical purity: observed specific rotation ÷ that of the pure enantiomer × 100.

Stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images. They share every physical property except the direction they rotate plane-polarized light, and they behave differently only toward other chiral things.
Describes two groups for which replacing each in turn gives a pair of enantiomers. They look identical in NMR but an enzyme or other chiral reagent can tell them apart.

terms.def: In a Diels–Alder reaction, the product in which the dienophile's electron-withdrawing group lay tucked under the diene in the transition state; with a cyclic diene it points toward the new C=C. It is usually the kinetic product. The other is exo.

A plot of free energy against reaction progress (the reaction coordinate). Peaks are transition states. A valley between two peaks is an intermediate; the levels at the two ends are the reactants and the products.
An alkene with an OH on one of its carbons (ene + ol). It is the tautomer of a ketone or aldehyde, and the keto form is usually far more stable.
The anion formed by removing an α hydrogen from a carbonyl compound. The negative charge is shared between the α carbon and the oxygen, and it usually reacts as a nucleophile through carbon.
Diastereomers that differ in configuration at only one of their stereocenters, such as D-glucose and D-mannose.

A three-membered cyclic ether, also called an oxirane. Ring strain makes it open easily: strong nucleophiles attack the less substituted carbon, while under acid the nucleophile usually goes to the more substituted carbon; either way it attacks from the back.
A bond on a chair cyclohexane that points outward, roughly along the ring's equator. Substituents prefer equatorial positions, where they avoid 1,3-diaxial interactions.
A carboxylic acid derivative in which the acid's OH is replaced by an OR group, R–CO–OR′.
A compound with an oxygen bonded to two carbon groups, R–O–R′.
Describes a step or reaction with ΔG° below zero: the products are lower in free energy, so equilibrium favors them. Endergonic is the reverse.
Describes a change that releases heat (ΔH below zero). Endothermic changes absorb heat (ΔH above zero).
More than eight valence electrons drawn around an atom of period 3 or below, such as sulfur in a sulfone or phosphorus in a phosphate. Period 2 atoms (C, N, O, F) never exceed an octet.
Separating compounds by shaking them between two liquids that do not mix, usually water and an organic solvent. Turning an acid or base into its charged form moves it into the water layer.
A long, unbranched carboxylic acid, usually with 12 to 20 carbons (an even number). Saturated fatty acids have no C=C; natural unsaturated ones have cis double bonds that kink the chain.
The crowded part of an IR spectrum below about 1500 cm⁻¹, full of bending and single-bond vibrations. It is unique to each compound but hard to interpret band by band.

The tie-breaking rule for numbering: write out the competing locant sets in order and compare them term by term; the set that is lower at the first place they differ wins. The same idea breaks ties between CIP priorities.
Making an ester from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol with an acid catalyst. It is an equilibrium, driven forward by using excess alcohol or removing water.
A flat cross drawing of stereocenters in which horizontal lines point toward you and vertical lines point away. Used mainly for sugars and amino acids.
A curved arrow with a single barb, showing one electron moving rather than a pair. Radical mechanisms are drawn with fishhooks.
The fluorenylmethoxycarbonyl group, a carbamate that protects an amine and is removed by a mild base (piperidine), so it is orthogonal to the acid-removed Boc.

The charge an atom would have if every bond's electrons were split equally: valence electrons minus (lone-pair electrons + number of bonds). The formal charges in a structure add up to its overall charge.
Attaching an acyl group to an aromatic ring with an acid chloride and AlCl₃, through an acylium ion, to give an aryl ketone. There is no rearrangement and the product does not react a second time.
Alkylating an aromatic ring with an alkyl halide and AlCl₃. The carbocation can rearrange, the product can react again, and strongly deactivated rings do not react.
A specific group of atoms within a molecule, such as –OH or C=O, that has characteristic reactions. Molecules with the same functional group react in similar ways.
Changing one functional group into another without changing the carbon skeleton, such as oxidizing an alcohol to a ketone. Abbreviated FGI.
Making a primary amine without over-alkylation: alkylate the phthalimide anion with a primary alkyl halide, then release the amine (with hydrazine or by hydrolysis).
A staggered conformation with the two largest groups 60° apart. Gauche butane is about 0.9 kcal/mol less stable than anti because of steric strain.
On the same carbon, as in a geminal dihalide or a gem-diol.
A lithium dialkylcuprate, R₂CuLi. It is a soft nucleophile: it adds 1,4 (conjugate addition) to enones, couples with organic halides and turns acid chlorides into ketones.
Tg, the temperature above which the amorphous regions of a polymer change from hard and glassy to soft and rubbery.

The bond from a sugar's anomeric carbon to another group: through oxygen (an acetal, often to another sugar's OH) or, in an N-glycosidic bond such as in nucleosides, through nitrogen. Its configuration and positions are written like α(1→4).

R–MgX, made from an organic halide and magnesium in dry ether. It adds to aldehydes and ketones to give alcohols, to esters twice, and to CO₂ to give carboxylic acids; water, alcohols or any acidic H destroy it.
The lowest-energy arrangement of the electrons in an atom or molecule.
A methyl ketone treated with excess halogen and base is cut into a carboxylate and CHX₃. With iodine the yellow iodoform precipitate is a test for methyl ketones.
The group 17 elements fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine. In organic molecules a halogen usually forms one bond and carries three lone pairs.
A compound with a halogen and an OH on neighboring carbons, made by adding X₂ to an alkene in water. The OH ends up on the more substituted carbon, anti to the halogen.

A transition state resembles whichever neighbor, reactants or products, is closer to it in energy. An uphill step has a late, product-like transition state; a downhill step an early, reactant-like one.

terms.term: hard and soft acids and bases
terms.def: Hard acids and bases are small, often highly charged and weakly polarizable; soft ones are large and polarizable. Hard partners react best with hard, soft with soft.
A flat drawing of a cyclic sugar seen edge-on. A group on the right in the Fischer projection points down in the Haworth projection.
The heat released when H₂ adds across a C=C. The less heat released, the more stable the alkene was, which is how alkene and diene stabilities are compared.
Palladium-catalyzed coupling of an aryl or vinyl halide with an alkene, replacing a vinylic hydrogen; it runs through migratory insertion and β-hydride elimination.
α-Bromination of a carboxylic acid with Br₂ and PBr₃, which works through the acyl bromide's enol.
A carbon bonded to both an OH and an OR, formed when one alcohol adds to an aldehyde or ketone. Open-chain hemiacetals are usually unstable; cyclic ones, as in sugars, are favored.
Bond breaking in which one atom keeps both bonding electrons, giving a cation and an anion. It is drawn with one full curved arrow.
Exhaustive methylation of an amine to a quaternary ammonium salt, then heating with hydroxide, which causes E2 to give mainly the less substituted alkene.
The less substituted alkene from an elimination. It is major when the base is bulky, such as tert-butoxide, or when the leaving group is a bulky trialkylammonium.
A primary amide treated with Br₂ and NaOH loses its carbonyl carbon and becomes a primary amine with one fewer carbon, through an isocyanate. The migrating group keeps its configuration.
The highest occupied molecular orbital: the highest-energy orbital that holds electrons. A nucleophile donates from its HOMO.
Bond breaking in which each atom keeps one of the two bonding electrons, giving two radicals. It is drawn with two fishhook arrows.
Describes two atoms or groups for which replacing either one gives the same compound. They are equivalent in every environment.

terms.def: A Wittig variant that uses a phosphonate-stabilized carbanion instead of a phosphonium ylide. It mainly gives E alkenes, often α,β-unsaturated esters.
A cyclic, planar, fully conjugated ring is aromatic if it has 4n + 2 π electrons and antiaromatic if it has 4n.
When electrons enter orbitals of equal energy, they occupy them one at a time with parallel spins before any orbital takes a second electron.
An orbital made by mixing s and p orbitals on one atom, such as sp³, sp² or sp. Hybrids point in definite directions, which sets the bond angles.
Mixing an atom's s and p orbitals into the same number of hybrid orbitals that point toward its bonds and lone pairs. Count the electron groups: four means sp³, three sp², two sp.
Addition of water across a C=C to make an alcohol. Acid-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov and goes through a carbocation, so it can rearrange.
H⁻, a hydrogen with two electrons. Reagents such as NaBH₄ and LiAlH₄ deliver it to carbonyl carbons; it is never present as a free ion in these reactions.
BH₃, then H₂O₂ and NaOH: adds H and OH across a C=C with the OH on the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov) and both on the same face (syn), with no rearrangement.

A strong dipole–dipole attraction between an H bonded to N, O or F (the donor) and a lone pair on another N, O or F (the acceptor). It explains why alcohols boil far higher than ethers of the same size.
Cleavage of a σ bond by H₂ over a catalyst, such as a benzyl ether giving toluene and an alcohol on H₂ and Pd/C. It removes benzyl and Cbz protecting groups.
The tendency of nonpolar groups to cluster together in water. It is driven mainly by entropy: clustering frees water molecules that were held in ordered cages around each nonpolar group.
Stabilizing overlap of a filled σ bond, usually C–H or C–C, with a neighboring empty or partly empty orbital, such as a carbocation's empty p orbital or an adjacent σ* orbital.
A compound with a C=N–R double bond, made from an aldehyde or ketone and a primary amine with loss of water, fastest near pH 4–5.
A C=N⁺ cation, the protonated or N-alkylated form of an imine. It is more electrophilic than a carbonyl.
The pull (or push) of electron density through σ bonds by a nearby electronegative (or electron-donating) group. It weakens quickly with distance and is small beyond about three bonds.
The area under a ¹H NMR signal, proportional to the number of hydrogens that produce it. It gives ratios, not absolute counts.
A species made in one step of a mechanism and used up in a later one. It sits in an energy valley and has a real, if short, lifetime, like a carbocation.
Attractions between separate molecules: London dispersion forces, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds. They set boiling point, melting point and solubility.

The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when one atom effectively transfers electrons to another. It is typical when the two atoms differ greatly in electronegativity, as in Na⁺Cl⁻.

Infrared spectroscopy: bonds absorb infrared light at frequencies matching their vibrations, so a spectrum shows which bonds and functional groups are present. A vibration absorbs only if it changes the dipole moment.
A compound R–N=C=O. Water adds to it to give a carbamic acid, which loses CO₂ to leave an amine; alcohols add to give carbamates.
The pH at which a molecule carries no net charge, written pI. For an amino acid with a neutral side chain it is the average of its two pKa values.
The substituent (CH₃)₂CH–, a three-carbon group attached through its middle carbon; its systematic name is propan-2-yl.
Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons, such as ¹²C and ¹³C, or hydrogen and deuterium.
The systematic naming rules of the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, which give every structure one unambiguous name built from prefixes, a root and a suffix.
CrO₃ in aqueous sulfuric acid (chromic acid). It oxidizes a primary alcohol all the way to the carboxylic acid, through the aldehyde's hydrate, and a secondary alcohol to a ketone.
A compound whose carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbons, R–CO–R′.
The enolate that forms faster, by removal of the more accessible α hydrogen; it is usually the less substituted one. LDA at −78 °C gives it.
A change in rate when an atom is swapped for an isotope. Replacing an H with D slows a step that breaks that C–H bond several-fold, which shows the bond breaks in the rate-determining step.
The product that forms fastest, through the lowest-energy transition state. It dominates under kinetic control: low temperature, where the reaction cannot reverse.
Heating sodium phenoxide with CO₂ under pressure, then acidifying, to put a COOH ortho to the OH, giving salicylic acid.
A cyclic amide, such as the four-membered β-lactam ring in penicillin.
A cyclic ester: the ester's C=O and O are both part of a ring.
The wavelength at which a compound absorbs most strongly in its UV-Vis spectrum.
Lithium diisopropylamide, a strong (pKaH about 36), bulky base that is a poor nucleophile. At −78 °C it converts a ketone completely and irreversibly into its kinetic enolate.
An equilibrium shifts to counteract a change imposed on it: removing a product, or adding excess reactant, drives the reaction forward.
The atom or group that departs from a molecule taking the old bond's electrons with it. Good leaving groups are weak bases, the conjugate bases of strong acids: I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, sulfonates and H₂O.
In water, any acid stronger than H₃O⁺ is converted completely to H₃O⁺, and any base stronger than OH⁻ to OH⁻, so the solvent caps how strong an acid or base can act in it.
An electron-pair acceptor, usually a species with an empty orbital, such as BF₃, AlCl₃, H⁺ or a carbocation.
An electron-pair donor, such as an amine, water or any anion with a lone pair.
A drawing that shows every valence electron in a molecule: shared pairs as bond lines, unshared pairs as dots, and any formal charges.

Lithium aluminum hydride, a powerful hydride donor that reduces aldehydes, ketones, esters and carboxylic acids to alcohols, and amides and nitriles to amines. It reacts violently with water, so it is used in dry ether with a separate aqueous workup.
A deliberately poisoned palladium catalyst that hydrogenates an alkyne only as far as the cis (Z) alkene.
Two electron groups on opposite sides of an atom, 180° apart, as at the sp carbons of an alkyne or the central carbon of CO₂.
A biomolecule defined by its solubility in nonpolar solvents rather than by one functional group: fats, oils, phospholipids, steroids, waxes and terpenes.
A chain-growth polymerization with no termination: chains keep growing as long as monomer remains, so adding a second monomer makes a block copolymer.
A number that gives the position of a substituent or functional group on the parent, such as the 2 in 2-methylpentane.
Weak attractions between temporary, induced dipoles. Every molecule has them, and they grow with size and surface contact, which is why longer alkanes boil higher.
A pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom and is not shared in a bond. Lone pairs are where most bases and nucleophiles donate from.
The lowest unoccupied molecular orbital: the lowest-energy empty orbital. An electrophile accepts electrons into its LUMO.
The mass-to-charge ratio of an ion. For the singly charged ions seen in most spectra it equals the ion's mass.
A peak two mass units above the molecular ion. Chlorine gives an M+2 about one third the height of M (3:1), and bromine gives M and M+2 of nearly equal height (1:1).
The local magnetic field set up by circulating π electrons. In an aromatic ring (the ring current) it deshields the ring's hydrogens, pushing them to about 7 to 8 ppm.
The resonance structure that most resembles the real hybrid. Rank them by: full octets first, then fewest formal charges, then any negative charge on the more electronegative atom.
Alkylate the enolate of diethyl malonate, then hydrolyze and heat to decarboxylate: the result is a substituted acetic acid, RCH₂COOH.
When HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the H goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens and X to the more substituted carbon, because that route goes through the more stable carbocation.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus. Isotopes of one element have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
A technique that ionizes molecules, often breaking them into fragments, and sorts the ions by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z). It gives the molecular weight and clues to structure.
A mass-spectrum fragmentation of a carbonyl compound with a γ hydrogen: that H moves to the oxygen through a six-membered transition state and the α–β bond breaks, losing a neutral alkene.
The step-by-step account of how a reaction happens: which bonds break and form, in what order, and which intermediates form along the way, drawn with curved arrows.
The resonance-stabilized anion (a cyclohexadienyl anion) formed when a nucleophile adds to an electron-poor aromatic ring in SNAr.
A compound with stereocenters that is achiral, because an internal plane of symmetry makes it identical to its mirror image. It is optically inactive and is not a racemate.
A substituent that withdraws electron density, such as –NO₂, C=O, –CN, –SO₃H or –NR₃⁺, and steers new electrophiles meta. Ortho or para attack would put positive charge right next to it.
A sphere of amphipathic molecules in water, with nonpolar tails packed inside and polar heads on the surface. Soap removes grease by trapping it in micelles.

Conjugate addition of a stabilized carbon nucleophile (the Michael donor, such as the enolate of a β-dicarbonyl) to an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl (the Michael acceptor), giving a 1,5-dicarbonyl compound.
How readily a group moves in a 1,2-shift. In the Baeyer–Villiger: H > tertiary > secondary ≈ cyclohexyl ≈ benzyl ≈ aryl > primary > methyl.
The radical cation M⁺• formed when a whole molecule loses one electron. Its m/z gives the molecular mass calculated with the most common isotope of each element (¹²C, ¹H, ³⁵Cl, ⁷⁹Br).

An orbital that spreads over two or more atoms, formed by combining atomic orbitals. Combining n atomic orbitals gives n molecular orbitals, some bonding (lower in energy) and some antibonding (higher).
A small molecule that joins with many others to form a polymer.
A simple sugar that cannot be hydrolyzed into smaller sugars, such as glucose or fructose. A disaccharide is two joined by a glycosidic bond; a polysaccharide is many.
The prefixes di-, tri-, tetra- (and bis-, tris- for complex substituents) that count identical substituents. They are ignored when substituents are put in alphabetical order.
A sequence of reactions that builds a target from available starting materials, planned so that every step's regiochemistry and stereochemistry are controlled.
The gradual change in specific rotation as the α and β anomers of a sugar interconvert through the open-chain form until they reach equilibrium (about 36% α : 64% β for glucose).
Sodium borohydride, a mild hydride donor that reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols but normally leaves esters, acids and amides alone. It can be used in alcohol solvents.
N-Bromosuccinimide, a reagent that keeps a low, steady concentration of Br₂ so that radical bromination occurs at allylic and benzylic positions instead of addition to a C=C.
Palladium- (or nickel-) catalyzed coupling of an organozinc compound with an organic halide.
A view straight down one C–C bond: the front carbon is the point where three bonds meet, and the back carbon is a circle with its three bonds sticking out from behind.
A compound with a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, R–C≡N. The nitrile carbon is at the same oxidation level as a carboxylic acid.
The group –NO₂, with nitrogen bonded to two oxygens and carrying formal charges (N⁺, one O⁻). It is strongly electron-withdrawing.
The rapid turning inside out of an amine's pyramid through a flat transition state. It is why most amines with three different groups cannot be separated into enantiomers.
A molecule with an odd molecular weight contains an odd number of nitrogen atoms; an even molecular weight means zero or an even number.
NO₂⁺, the electrophile in aromatic nitration, made from nitric acid and sulfuric acid.
Nuclear magnetic resonance: nuclei such as ¹H and ¹³C in a strong magnetic field absorb radio waves at frequencies set by their electronic surroundings, which reveals the carbon–hydrogen framework.
A point or plane where an orbital's wavefunction is zero, so the electron is never found there. The two lobes of a p orbital are separated by a nodal plane.
Describes a ring that fails one of the first three tests (cyclic, planar, fully conjugated), for example because an sp³ ring carbon breaks the conjugation.
An electron-rich species that donates a pair of electrons to an electrophile to form a new bond. Anions, neutral molecules with lone pairs and π bonds can all act as nucleophiles.
Addition–elimination at an acyl carbon: a nucleophile adds to give a tetrahedral intermediate, which collapses to expel the leaving group. Reactivity runs acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide.
The core carbonyl reaction: a nucleophile bonds to the carbonyl carbon, the π bond's electrons move onto oxygen to give a tetrahedral alkoxide, and that oxygen is then protonated.

A nucleophile replaces a leaving group on an aromatic ring that carries strong electron-withdrawing groups ortho or para to it. Addition comes first, giving a Meisenheimer complex; fluoride is the best leaving group here.
A reaction in which a nucleophile replaces a leaving group on a carbon. It happens by SN2 or SN1.

How fast a nucleophile reacts, a rate property, unlike basicity, which is an equilibrium one. It rises with negative charge and polarizability and falls with electronegativity, steric bulk and strong solvation.
A nitrogen base joined to a ribose or 2-deoxyribose through an N-glycosidic bond at the sugar's anomeric carbon. A nucleotide is a nucleoside with one or more phosphates.
Second-row atoms (C, N, O, F) are most stable with eight valence electrons around them, counting both shared bonding pairs and lone pairs. Hydrogen is full with two.
The rotation of plane-polarized light by a sample that contains more of one enantiomer than the other. Clockwise rotation is labeled (+), counterclockwise (−); neither is linked to R or S.
A region of space around a nucleus (or a molecule) where an electron is likely to be found. Each orbital holds at most two electrons.
R–Li, such as butyllithium: more reactive and more basic than a Grignard reagent, and often used at −78 °C.
A compound with a carbon–metal bond. The carbon is δ− and behaves like a carbanion: a strong base and a carbon nucleophile.
Positions on a benzene ring relative to an existing substituent: ortho is the next carbon (1,2), meta is two carbons away (1,3) and para is directly opposite (1,4).

A substituent that sends a new electrophile to the ortho and para positions: every activator, and the halogens, which are weakly deactivating. A lone pair or alkyl group next to the ring stabilizes the arenium ion for ortho/para attack.
Protecting groups that come off under different conditions, so each can be removed without disturbing the others.
In organic chemistry, a gain of bonds from carbon to more electronegative atoms (O, N, halogens) or a loss of C–H bonds, such as alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid.
A carbon's bookkeeping charge: +1 for each bond to a more electronegative atom, −1 for each bond to hydrogen, 0 for each bond to carbon. It places a carbon on the oxidation ladder.
A metal inserts into a bond such as C–X, gaining two ligands and raising its oxidation state by two, as Pd(0) becomes Pd(II).
A cation in which a positive carbon is bonded to an oxygen that shares a lone pair with it, C=O⁺R ↔ ⁺C–OR. It is the key intermediate in acetal formation and glycoside chemistry.
A positively charged oxygen with three bonds and one lone pair, such as H₃O⁺ or a protonated alcohol, R–OH₂⁺.
Markovnikov addition of water to an alkene using Hg(OAc)₂ in water, then NaBH₄. It goes through a bridged mercurinium ion, so it does not rearrange.
Cleavage of a C=C with ozone, O₃. A reductive workup (Me₂S or Zn) gives aldehydes and ketones; an oxidative workup (H₂O₂) turns any aldehyde into a carboxylic acid.

The chain whose length gives a name its root: the longest continuous chain of carbons, except that once a principal characteristic group is present, the parent must contain it. When two chains tie, take the one with more substituents.
A fraction of a full charge on an atom in a polar bond, written δ+ or δ−. The more electronegative atom carries δ−.
No two electrons in an atom can be in exactly the same state, so one orbital holds at most two electrons and they must have opposite spins.
Phosphorus tribromide, which turns a primary or secondary alcohol into an alkyl bromide by SN2, with inversion and no rearrangement.
Pyridinium chlorochromate, used in CH₂Cl₂ with no water. It oxidizes a primary alcohol to the aldehyde and stops there, and a secondary alcohol to a ketone.

The amide bond linking the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amino group of the next. Resonance gives it partial double-bond character, so it is planar, does not rotate freely and is usually trans.
A concerted reaction that passes through a cyclic transition state with no intermediates: cycloadditions, electrocyclic reactions and sigmatropic rearrangements.
With peroxides present, HBr adds to an alkene anti-Markovnikov by a radical chain: Br• adds first, to the less substituted carbon, so that the more stable radical forms.
A carboxylic acid with an extra oxygen, RCO₃H, such as mCPBA. It transfers one oxygen to an alkene in a single syn step, giving an epoxide.
The sign, + or −, of an orbital's wavefunction in a region, usually shown by shading the lobes. Overlap of lobes with the same phase builds a bond; overlap of opposite phases does not.
A compound with an OH bonded directly to an aromatic ring. Phenol (pKa about 10) is far more acidic than an alcohol because the phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilized.
The conjugate base of a phenol, ArO⁻, whose negative charge is spread into the ring by resonance. It is a strongly activated ring and a good nucleophile.
A benzene ring used as a substituent, C₆H₅–, abbreviated Ph.
The link in a nucleic acid backbone: a phosphate esterified to the 3′-OH of one sugar and the 5′-OH of the next. A strand is read from its 5′ end to its 3′ end.
A lipid with two fatty acid chains and a polar phosphate-containing head group. Phospholipids form the bilayers of cell membranes.
A reaction driven by absorbed light rather than by heat. The photon lifts an electron from the HOMO to the LUMO, which reverses the conrotatory/disrotatory choice of an electrocyclic reaction.

A bond made by side-by-side overlap of two parallel p orbitals, with its electron density above and below the bond axis. It blocks rotation and its electrons are exposed, so it is the reactive part of a C=C.
Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid with sodium chlorite (NaClO₂) under mild acid, with a scavenger to mop up the HOCl byproduct. It leaves C=C bonds alone.
The negative base-10 logarithm of Ka. A lower pKa means a stronger acid, and each unit is a tenfold difference in strength. Acid–base equilibria favor the side with the weaker acid (higher pKa).
The pKa of a base's conjugate acid, used to rank bases: the higher the pKaH, the stronger the base.
A plane that cuts a molecule into two halves that are mirror images of each other. A molecule that has one, in any conformation it can reach, is achiral.
A small molecule mixed into a polymer to push chains apart, lowering its glass transition temperature and making it softer and more flexible.
A polar solvent with no O–H or N–H bonds, such as acetone, DMSO, DMF or acetonitrile. Anions stay poorly solvated and reactive in it, so it speeds SN2.

A covalent bond whose electrons are shared unequally because the two atoms differ in electronegativity, leaving the atoms with partial charges. C–O, C–N and C–Cl are polar; C–C and C–H are essentially nonpolar.
A polar solvent with O–H or N–H bonds, such as water, methanol or ethanol. It hydrogen-bonds to anions, which slows small anionic nucleophiles and stabilizes ions, so it favors SN1 and E1.
How easily an atom's electron cloud is distorted. It grows down a group as atoms get larger, which lets a big atom such as iodine spread a charge or an electron pair over more space.
A polymer whose repeat units are joined by amide links, made from a diacid (or acid chloride) and a diamine, such as nylon or Kevlar.
A polymer joined by carbonate links, –O–CO–O–, such as the one made from bisphenol A and phosgene.
A polymer whose repeat units are joined by ester links, made from a diacid (or its derivative) and a diol, such as PET.
A large molecule built from many repeating smaller units (monomers) joined by covalent bonds.
A chain of amino acid residues joined by peptide bonds, written from the N-terminus (free NH₂) to the C-terminus (free COOH). A protein is one or more long polypeptides.
A polymer joined by carbamate (urethane) links, made by adding a diol to a diisocyanate without losing any small molecule.
The sequence of amino acids in a protein chain, held by covalent peptide bonds.

Degree of substitution: a carbon bonded to one other carbon is primary (1°), to two secondary (2°), to three tertiary (3°), to four quaternary (4°). Alcohols and halides take the label of their carbon; amines count the carbons on the nitrogen.
The highest-priority functional group in a molecule. It is named as the suffix and gets the lowest possible locant; every other group becomes a prefix.
Able to become chiral in one step: an sp³ atom with two identical groups, one of which could be replaced, or a flat sp² carbon whose two faces give different products when attacked.

terms.def: A group that temporarily masks a reactive functional group so it survives a reaction elsewhere in the molecule, and is removed afterward: protect, react, deprotect.
A step in which an H⁺ moves from an acid to a base: one curved arrow from the base to the H, one from the H–A bond onto A.
A base with two fused rings, adenine (A) or guanine (G). Pyrimidines have one ring: cytosine (C), thymine (T) and uracil (U).
The six-membered ring form of a sugar (five carbons and one oxygen). A furanose is the five-membered ring form.

A benzene-like aromatic ring with one CH replaced by N. The nitrogen's lone pair lies in the ring plane, outside the π system, so it is free to take a proton: pyridine is a base (pKaH about 5.2), though weaker than alkylamines because the lone pair sits in an sp² orbital.
A five-membered aromatic ring containing an NH. The nitrogen's lone pair is part of the six-electron aromatic system, so pyrrole is hardly basic at all.
A salt R₄N⁺ X⁻ whose nitrogen carries four carbon groups and a positive charge, with no lone pair and no N–H.
A six-membered ring with two C=O groups, most often para to each other (cyclohexa-2,5-diene-1,4-dione), made by oxidizing a hydroquinone. Reduction turns it back.
The label for a stereocenter: with the lowest-priority group pointing away, trace priorities 1 → 2 → 3. Clockwise is R, counterclockwise is S.
A 50:50 mixture of two enantiomers. It rotates plane-polarized light by zero, though each molecule in it is chiral.
Conversion of a single enantiomer into a racemic mixture, as happens when a reaction passes through a flat carbocation or an enol.
A species with an unpaired electron, such as Br• or CH₃•. Carbon radicals have only seven valence electrons and are usually very reactive.
A radical reaction in three stages: initiation (radicals are created), propagation (each step consumes one radical and makes another, forming the product) and termination (two radicals combine).
Replacement of an alkane C–H with C–Cl or C–Br by a radical chain mechanism, started by light or heat. Bromination is highly selective for the most substituted C–H; chlorination is not.
A compound with a weak bond that breaks easily on heating or with light, such as a peroxide or AIBN, giving the first radicals of a chain.
The step of a multistep mechanism whose transition state is highest in energy. It limits the overall rate and sets the rate law.
Labels for the two faces of a trigonal carbon with three different groups: looking at one face, if priorities 1 → 2 → 3 run clockwise it is the Re face, counterclockwise the Si face.

terms.def: A sugar with a free hemiacetal (free anomeric carbon), which can open to the free carbonyl form and give a positive Tollens' or Benedict's test. Sucrose, with both anomeric carbons tied up, is a non-reducing sugar.
The reverse of oxidation: a gain of C–H bonds or a loss of bonds from carbon to O, N or halogens, such as ketone → alcohol.
Combining an aldehyde or ketone with an amine to form an imine or iminium ion, which is reduced in the same pot (often by NaBH₃CN) to an amine with one more carbon group on nitrogen.
Two groups on a metal bond to each other and leave, lowering the metal's oxidation state by two. In cross-coupling this step makes the new C–C bond and regenerates Pd(0).
Describes a reaction that favors one of two possible orientations, putting a new group on one particular atom, such as Markovnikov addition.
The smallest piece of a polymer's structure that repeats along the chain, drawn in brackets with a subscript n.
Separation of a racemic mixture into its two enantiomers, usually by reacting it with a single enantiomer of another compound to make separable diastereomers.
The extra stability that delocalization gives a molecule, measured as the gap between its expected and actual heat of hydrogenation; benzene's is about 36 kcal/mol (150 kJ/mol).
The real electronic structure of a species that has resonance structures: a weighted blend of them, with electrons spread over several atoms.

Two or more Lewis structures for one species that differ only in where π electrons and lone pairs are placed, with every atom in the same position. The real species is one hybrid of them, not a flicker between them.
A structural pattern in a target that points to a particular disconnection, such as a β-hydroxy carbonyl pointing to an aldol.

Planning a synthesis backward: from the target, make imaginary cuts (disconnections) that each match a known reaction, until you reach simple starting materials. A retrosynthetic step is drawn with a double-lined arrow, ⇒.
The interconversion of one chair cyclohexane into the other by rotation about ring bonds. Every axial position becomes equatorial and vice versa, but a group that pointed up still points up.

The extra energy of a ring compared with an unstrained open chain, made up of angle strain, torsional strain and steric strain. It is large in cyclopropane and cyclobutane and essentially zero in the chair of cyclohexane.
A Michael addition followed by an intramolecular aldol condensation, which builds a new six-membered ring containing an α,β-unsaturated ketone.

The share of a hybrid orbital that comes from the s orbital: 25% for sp³, 33% for sp² and 50% for sp. More s-character holds electrons closer to the nucleus, so bonds are shorter and an anion in that orbital is more stable.
The two conformations of a conjugated diene about its central single bond: s-cis has both double bonds on the same side, s-trans on opposite sides. Only the s-cis can do a Diels–Alder reaction.
Replacing the N₂⁺ of an aryl diazonium salt with Cl, Br or CN using the copper(I) salt CuCl, CuBr or CuCN.

Hydrolysis of an ester by hydroxide, giving a carboxylate salt and an alcohol. It does not reverse, because the acid formed is at once deprotonated to a carboxylate that the alcohol cannot attack; it is how soap is made from fats.
Holding as many hydrogens as its carbons allow: no π bonds. Unsaturated compounds have C=C or C≡C bonds (and, counted from a formula, rings).
Heating an aryl diazonium tetrafluoroborate, ArN₂⁺ BF₄⁻, to make an aryl fluoride.
Regular local folding of a protein backbone held by N–H···O=C hydrogen bonds: mainly the α-helix and the β-sheet.

A nucleus surrounded by more electron density is shielded and comes into resonance upfield (lower δ); one stripped of electron density, as near O or a halogen, is deshielded and appears downfield (higher δ).
A carbocation rearrangement in which a hydrogen (as hydride) or an alkyl group moves with its bonding pair from a neighboring carbon to the cationic carbon, usually giving a more stable carbocation.
Hot KMnO₄ (or chromic acid) oxidizes any alkyl side chain that has a benzylic hydrogen down to a –COOH on the ring, whatever its length.
A bond whose electron density lies along the line joining the two nuclei, made by head-on overlap. Every single bond is a σ bond, and every double or triple bond contains exactly one.

A pericyclic reaction in which one σ bond breaks and another forms further along a π system, as the π bonds shift, all in one step. It is named [i,j] by counting atoms out from each end of the bond that breaks.
An alcohol protected as R–O–SiR₃, such as a TBS ether. It survives bases, Grignard reagents and oxidants, and is removed with fluoride (TBAF) or acid.
Cyclopropanation of an alkene with CH₂I₂ and a zinc–copper couple, Zn(Cu). The carbenoid ICH₂ZnI adds a CH₂ in one syn step, so the reaction is stereospecific.
A drawing in which every line end and bend is a carbon, hydrogens on carbon are not drawn, and every other atom is written out with its hydrogens.

Unimolecular nucleophilic substitution: the leaving group departs first to give a carbocation (the slow step), then the nucleophile adds to either face. Rate = k[substrate]; favored at 3°, allylic and benzylic carbons in polar protic solvents.

Bimolecular nucleophilic substitution: in one concerted step the nucleophile attacks from the back as the leaving group leaves, inverting the carbon. Rate = k[Nu][substrate]; fastest at methyl and 1° carbons, impossible at 3°.
Thionyl chloride, which turns a primary or secondary alcohol into an alkyl chloride, and a carboxylic acid into an acid chloride, releasing SO₂ and HCl.
Building a peptide on a resin bead from the C-terminus: protect, couple (with DCC or a similar reagent), deprotect, wash, repeat, then cleave from the resin. Also called Merrifield synthesis.
The clustering of solvent molecules around a dissolved species, especially an ion, which stabilizes it. Small, concentrated charges are solvated most strongly.
A substitution (or elimination) in which the solvent itself, such as water or an alcohol, is the nucleophile or base.
Palladium- and copper-catalyzed coupling of a terminal alkyne with an aryl or vinyl halide.
One s and one p orbital mixed into two sp orbitals 180° apart, leaving two p orbitals free for π bonds. An atom with two electron groups, such as a triple-bonded carbon, is sp.
One s and two p orbitals mixed into three sp² orbitals lying in a plane 120° apart, leaving one unhybridized p orbital perpendicular to that plane. An atom with three electron groups is sp².
One s and three p orbitals mixed into four sp³ orbitals pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart. An atom with four electron groups is sp³.
The rotation a chiral compound gives under standard conditions: the observed rotation divided by path length (dm) and concentration (g/mL), written [α].
Splitting of an NMR signal by hydrogens on neighboring atoms: n equivalent neighbors split it into n + 1 peaks (singlet, doublet, triplet, quartet...).
A conformation in which each bond on the front carbon sits halfway between two on the back (dihedral angles of 60°). It is the low-energy arrangement.
Polymerization in which any two molecules with complementary groups can react, so chains grow by joining fragments; high molar mass appears only at very high conversion.
An atom at which swapping any two groups gives a stereoisomer. The common case is an sp³ carbon bearing four different groups.
Isomers with the same atoms joined in the same order but arranged differently in space. Enantiomers and diastereomers are the two kinds.
Describes a reaction that forms one stereoisomer in preference to others when more than one could form.
Describes a reaction in which stereoisomeric starting materials give stereoisomerically different products, by a mechanism that sets the outcome, such as inversion in SN2 or anti elimination in E2.
Crowding around a reacting atom that blocks a reagent's approach and slows the reaction, as bulky groups do to SN2 at a tertiary carbon.
The extra energy when atoms or groups are pushed closer together than their sizes allow, so their electron clouds repel.
A lipid built on four fused rings, three six-membered and one five-membered, such as cholesterol.
Palladium-catalyzed coupling of an organotin compound (an organostannane) with an organic halide.
An acid that gives up its proton essentially completely in water, such as HCl, HBr, HI or H₂SO₄. Its conjugate base is extremely weak.
An atom or group attached to the parent chain in place of a hydrogen, named as a prefix such as methyl- or chloro-.
The molecule a reagent acts on. In substitution and elimination it is the compound that carries the leaving group, such as an alkyl halide.
The ending of a name that states the principal characteristic group, such as -ol for an alcohol, -one for a ketone or -oic acid for a carboxylic acid.
An ester R–O–SO₂R′ such as a tosylate (OTs), mesylate (OMs) or triflate (OTf). Making one turns an alcohol's poor OH leaving group into an excellent one without touching the C–O bond.
Adding an SO₃H group to an aromatic ring with SO₃ in sulfuric acid (fuming sulfuric acid). Because it is reversible, a sulfonic acid group can be used as a removable blocking group.
Palladium-catalyzed coupling of an organoboron compound, such as a boronic acid, with an aryl or vinyl halide in the presence of base. It is the classic way to make biaryls.
Oxidation with DMSO and oxalyl chloride, then Et₃N, at −78 °C: a primary alcohol gives the aldehyde and a secondary alcohol the ketone, with no chromium.
Adding an OH to each carbon of a C=C from the same face, with OsO₄ (often catalytic, with NMO) or cold dilute KMnO₄, to give a 1,2-diol.
An idealized fragment, often an ion, produced by a disconnection. The synthetic equivalent is the real reagent that plays its part, such as a Grignard reagent for an R⁻ synthon.
The stereochemical pattern of substituents along a polymer chain: isotactic (all on one side), syndiotactic (alternating) or atactic (random).

Constitutional isomers that interconvert quickly by moving a proton and shifting a double bond, such as a ketone and its enol. They are different compounds, not resonance structures, because an atom moves.
An alkyne at the end of a chain, R–C≡C–H. Its sp C–H is unusually acidic (pKa about 25). An internal alkyne has carbon groups on both ends.
A natural product built from five-carbon isoprene units, usually joined head to tail.
The substituent (CH₃)₃C–, attached through a carbon that carries three methyl groups. Its bulk makes it a common steric blocker.
The overall 3D fold of one protein chain, held by the hydrophobic effect, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and disulfide bonds. Quaternary structure is the arrangement of several chains together.
The shape of four electron groups around an atom, pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron about 109.5° apart, as in methane.
The sp³ species formed when a nucleophile adds to a carbonyl carbon. In acyl substitution it collapses, re-forming the C=O and expelling a leaving group.
The more stable, usually more substituted enolate. It dominates when the enolates can interconvert: a weaker base, a little free ketone or proton source, and higher temperature.
The most stable product. It dominates under thermodynamic control: higher temperature, where every step can reverse and the products reach equilibrium.
A polymer that softens when heated and can be remelted and reshaped, because its chains are not cross-linked.
A polymer that is cured into a cross-linked network and does not melt on reheating.
The sulfur analog of an alcohol, R–SH.
Tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄, the NMR reference compound whose signal is set at δ = 0.
Warming a sample with Tollens' reagent, Ag(NH₃)₂⁺ in aqueous ammonia: an aldehyde is oxidized and the silver is reduced to a metallic mirror. Ordinary ketones give no mirror.
The extra energy of eclipsed bonds on neighboring atoms compared with staggered ones.
Exchange of an ester's OR group for a different alcohol's OR, under acid or base catalysis.
The highest-energy point of one reaction step, with bonds partly made and partly broken. It has no lifetime and cannot be isolated; it is marked ‡.
Transfer of an organic group from one metal (boron, tin, zinc) to another, such as palladium, in a coupling cycle.
A triester of glycerol with three fatty acids. Fats are solid triglycerides rich in saturated chains; oils are liquid ones rich in cis-unsaturated chains.
The shape of three electron groups around an atom, lying flat and 120° apart, as at an sp² carbon or a carbocation.
The shape of an atom with three bonds and one lone pair, such as the nitrogen in ammonia: a squat pyramid with bond angles near 107°.
Three shared electron pairs between two atoms: one σ bond and two π bonds at right angles to each other. Both atoms are sp and the arrangement is linear.
Polarity reversal: turning a normally electrophilic carbon into a nucleophilic one, as when the δ+ carbon of an alkyl halide becomes the δ− carbon of a Grignard reagent.
Describes a step whose rate depends on the concentration of only one species, like the ionization in SN1 and E1. A bimolecular step depends on two.

Measuring which ultraviolet and visible wavelengths a compound absorbs, mainly by promoting a π electron from the HOMO to the LUMO. The longer the conjugated system, the longer the wavelength absorbed.
The electrons in an atom's outermost shell, which form its bonds and lone pairs. Carbon has 4, nitrogen 5, oxygen 6 and each halogen 7.
On neighboring carbons (a 1,2 relationship), as in a vicinal dihalide or a vicinal diol.
A compound with OH groups on neighboring carbons, also called a 1,2-diol or glycol.
The substituent CH₂=CH–, an alkene carbon attached directly to the rest of the molecule.
Valence shell electron pair repulsion: the electron groups around an atom spread as far apart as possible, and that arrangement sets the molecule's shape.
Heating natural rubber with sulfur to form sulfur cross-links between chains, which makes it elastic rather than sticky.
The inversion of configuration in SN2: the three groups that stay on the carbon flip over like an umbrella in the wind. The R/S letter may or may not change, because priorities can change too.
The number of waves per centimeter (1/wavelength), in cm⁻¹, used for IR positions. Higher wavenumbers mean higher energy: stronger, stiffer bonds and lighter atoms vibrate higher.
An acid that gives up only a small fraction of its protons in water at equilibrium, such as acetic acid. Its conjugate base is a reasonable base.
The convention for drawing 3D shape on paper: a solid wedge is a bond coming toward you, a hashed (dashed) wedge is a bond going away, and a plain line lies in the plane of the page.
An N-methoxy-N-methyl amide. A Grignard or organolithium adds to it only once, because the metal holds the tetrahedral intermediate together, so workup gives a ketone.
Making an ether by SN2 between an alkoxide and a methyl or primary alkyl halide (or sulfonate). Choose the half with the less hindered carbon to carry the leaving group.
An aldehyde or ketone plus a phosphorus ylide (Ph₃P=CR₂) gives an alkene and Ph₃P=O. The new C=C forms exactly where the C=O was.
Conversion of an aldehyde or ketone's C=O into CH₂ with hydrazine and strong base (KOH) on heating, through a hydrazone. It is the basic-conditions partner of the Clemmensen reduction.
Empirical rules that estimate λmax for a conjugated diene or enone: start from a base value and add fixed increments for ring residues, exocyclic double bonds and extra conjugated C=C.

Orbital-symmetry rules for concerted reactions. For an electrocyclic reaction: 4n π electrons go conrotatory with heat and disrotatory with light; 4n + 2 go disrotatory with heat and conrotatory with light.
The steps after the main reaction that quench leftover reagents and isolate the product, such as adding aqueous acid (H₃O⁺) to protonate an alkoxide.
A neutral species with a positive and a negative charge on adjacent atoms, each with a full octet, such as Ph₃P⁺–C⁻H₂.
An elimination usually gives the more substituted, more stable alkene as the major product.
A titanium–aluminum catalyst that polymerizes alkenes such as propene by repeated insertion at a metal site, giving stereoregular (for example isotactic) chains with little branching.
A neutral molecule that carries a positive and a negative charge on different atoms, such as an amino acid near neutral pH, H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻.
